data.name: Max, an Autistic Journey
data.detailed_description:
Max, an Autistic Journey is a retro style top-down turn-based RPG filled with mini games, monsters and most of all, heart. Developed by Stéphane Cantin, who is just a devoted dad who made a game with his son about his son’s autism.

During the game player’s step into the shoes of Max, a ten year old boy who must find ways to deal with everyday life while being diagnosed with an autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Many players will discover a world familiar but alien to them. Some may relate to Max's story all too well. Regardless where you fall in the spectrum of life, Max, an Autistic Journey delivers an entertaining, imaginative and informative trip worth taking.

This retro-inspired RPG gives players not only a unique gaming experience, but an insight into a world many people have never seen. While the visualization of the beasts may be fantasy, the emotions and frustrations they represent are very real for a lot of people.


There are few greater inspirations in life than one's love of their child. Max, an Autistic Journey is Stéphane’s inspired interactive love letter about his son Max who was born with autism that he worked hand in hand with throughout the development of the title. While there is a wide spectrum of autism, this game focuses on Max, where he falls in that spectrum and how he experiences and deals with daily life.


  • Classic turn-based battle system featuring clever weapons and special abilities to confront monstrous manifestations of emotions and anxieties
  • Gain experience points through imaginary toy battles and by confronting your fears and anxieties to level up
  • Core retro RPG mechanics infused with multiple Mini Games such as picture puzzles, race cars and making music
  • Endearing tale of trials and tribulations from a unique perspective that inspires, educates and entertains as the story unfolds
  • Mouse & Keyboard and Full Controller Support
  • Steam Achievements, Cloud Saves & Steam Trading Cards

The developer will be donating a portion of proceeds from game sales to the Miriam Foundation, a charitable organization that helps people with autism spectrum disorders and intellectual disabilities lead fulfilling lives.

reviews.review:
Max, an Autistic Journey is one of those rare independent games that immediately distinguishes itself through subject matter alone. Developed by Professional Imagination and published by GPAC, the title places players in the role of Max, a young boy living with Autism Spectrum Disorder, and attempts to translate his daily experiences into an accessible retro-inspired RPG adventure. Rather than building its identity around epic quests or world-saving stakes, the game focuses on something much smaller yet arguably more meaningful: navigating a single day in the life of a child whose routines, anxieties, and imagination shape how he perceives the world.

The game's premise is simple but effective. Players guide Max through everyday activities such as waking up, getting dressed, eating breakfast, attending school, and interacting with family and friends. However, these ordinary tasks are reframed through Max's perspective. His imagination transforms challenges into turn-based battles against monsters, while a constantly monitored anxiety meter reflects his emotional state throughout the day. This mechanic serves as the centerpiece of the experience, reinforcing the importance of routine and demonstrating how disruptions can significantly affect someone on the autism spectrum. It is a thoughtful concept that elevates what could have been a standard RPG Maker project into something with a more personal and educational purpose.

From a gameplay standpoint, Max, an Autistic Journey borrows heavily from classic top-down role-playing games. Combat encounters are straightforward, utilizing familiar commands such as Attack, Specials, Magic, Guard, and Items. The title supplements its RPG framework with numerous minigames, including searching for clothes, navigating traffic, collecting objects, and completing timed tasks. These activities help maintain variety across the relatively short campaign, though their execution is admittedly inconsistent. Some minigames successfully immerse players in Max's world, while others feel simplistic and occasionally repetitive. Still, there is a genuine sincerity behind their inclusion, as they are designed less to challenge the player mechanically and more to illustrate everyday situations through Max's eyes.

Visually, the game embraces a retro pixel-art aesthetic reminiscent of RPG Maker titles from the early 2010s. Environments are colorful, character sprites are expressive enough for the game's tone, and the presentation complements the childlike wonder of Max's imagination. The soundtrack similarly supports the experience with gentle compositions that emphasize warmth rather than drama. While no individual element stands out as technically exceptional, the audiovisual package works because it remains focused on supporting the narrative. The modest production values are understandable given the project's independent origins, and the game's emotional ambitions often compensate for its technical limitations.

What ultimately makes Max, an Autistic Journey noteworthy is its authenticity. The game was inspired by creator Stéphane Cantin's own experiences with his autistic son, and that personal connection is evident throughout the adventure. Rather than portraying autism as a superpower or relying on stereotypes, the game presents it as a part of Max's identity—one that comes with challenges, fears, routines, and moments of joy. It doesn't claim to represent every autistic individual, nor could it, but it succeeds in encouraging empathy and understanding. For parents, educators, or players interested in seeing how games can tackle neurodiversity in meaningful ways, there is undeniable value in what Professional Imagination has accomplished.

That said, players expecting deep RPG mechanics or polished gameplay systems may find themselves disappointed. Combat lacks complexity, exploration is limited, and the overall experience can occasionally feel more like an interactive educational tool than a traditional video game. The pacing also suffers in places, particularly when certain minigames overstay their welcome. Yet criticizing Max, an Autistic Journey solely on conventional gaming standards risks overlooking its primary objective. This is a game built around communication and awareness first, entertainment second.

In the end, Max, an Autistic Journey succeeds because of its heart. It is an imperfect but admirable title that uses the interactive nature of games to foster empathy in a way few developers have attempted. Its strongest moments are not found in battles or level progression, but in the quiet realization that everyday experiences can feel vastly different depending on who is living them. More than a decade after its release, it remains a notable example of how indie developers can explore deeply personal stories through the medium of video games.

Rating: 7/10
